title: Biscuits Consumption in Early-Life Induces Metabolic Alterations, Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Hepatic Steatosis and Elevated Pro-Inflammatory Cytokines in Wistar Rats
content:
Introduction: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) among children and adolescents is a growing global health challenge. MetS is linked to ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and associates with metabolic-dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).  This study investigated the impacts of early-life consumption of milk-containing biscuits (MCB) and chocolate-containing biscuits (CCB) on glucose and lipid homeostasis and risk of MASLD.
Materials and Methods: Fifteen male Wistar rats aged 28-42 days (77–112 g) were fed with a standard diet (SD) and served as control, SD+4.03 g/kg body weight of three brands of minced MCB, or CCB for six weeks. Biscuits’ nutritional and caloric contents (BNC), fasting blood glucose (FBG) and insulin, triglyceride-glucose index (TyG), homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), liver index, pro-inflammatory cytokines, hepatic and plasma lipid profile were determined using standard methods. NBC was compared using independent t-test and group difference by one-way ANOVA and post-hoc test; significance set at p < 0.05. 
Results: MCB and CCB had comparable macronutrients and calories. Compared to the control, biscuit-exposed rats had hypertriglyceridaemia, significantly higher liver index, TyG, TNF-a, IL-6, hepatic total cholesterol and triglyceride levels. The CCB group showed significantly lower insulin, higher FBG, HOMA-IR, VLDL-C and LDL-C. 
Conclusion: Biscuit intake in early-life causes metabolic abnormalities, insulin resistance, hepatic steatosis and upregulated pro-inflammatory cytokines. Disruptions of glucose and lipids homeostasis are more evident in CCB. Findings suggest that frequent and substantial intake of such biscuits by preschool children, particularly those with underlying metabolic-related conditions, may be at risk of developing MetS or MASLD later in life. Integrating early-life nutrition education into preschool health programmes will be critical to achieving SDG 3.4 and promoting lifelong metabolic health.
